items.title: Holman Bill — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: That was when I first joined Charlie.

ctx.x: Yeah. That was when I first joined Charlie. I always think of it as 1951, but that was our first road trip. I wanted to say something about him, because I think he was a wonderful guy to work with. His book had all these lovely charts. He had things by Manny Albam, [Neil] Hefti, Andy Gibson. I don‟t know who all wrote the charts, but he‟d collected these tunes through the years. So they were a distillation of his taste, and it was really good. I liked working with him.
How did you get in the band?

items.title: 52150_Charlie Barnet oral history interview
items.q: Billy Byers, Bill Holman, and -- well, they did the majority of them.

ctx.x: Oh, a whole bunch -- well, let's see, Billy Byers, Bill Holman, and -- well, they did the majority of them. And of course there's a montage there that was really a collection of parts out of different arrangements, you know. Andy Gibson, William Moore, Jr., and Billy May. And then there's -- let's see, there's, "Jeeps Blues," on there, the original Ellington arrangement, with Willy Smith doing it this time. And Clarke Terry does his Mumbles with the big band.
Gee, that would be great to see and hear here.

items.title: Bill Holman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999
items.q: this was ’51 when I worked with Charlie. He wasn’t really buying charts then but I had this chart that I wrote for him and I put it in the book

ctx.x: Well it looks like one of your first assignments, with Charlie Barnet, were you still in college at that time?

No. I got out of school I think about 1950, and this was ’51 when I worked with Charlie. He wasn’t really buying charts then but I had this chart that I wrote for him and I put it in the book and after a while I guess the guilt got to him or something and he paid me for it, but he was kind of winding his career down at that time, and he didn’t want to invest a whole lot more into it. But then later in the 50s I did a couple of albums for him for the Everest label. So I got to write for him finally.
Were you making more money with your instrument or more money with your pen?
